t.en: In <level-ref to="seam"></level-ref> you worked out the seam table. This level you actually cut seams out.
You find the first seam: click the smallest cell in the bottom row, then trace back up row by row. Of the three candidates on the row above, which one did the seam come from?

Once a seam is cut, the picture is a column narrower, and the energy and seam table have to be worked out again. Leave the remaining seams to the machine, 8 in all. At the end, compare the result with simply squashing the picture.

goal.en: Find the lowest-energy seam and cut it out. Cut 8 seams in all, making the picture 8 columns narrower.

how.en: Trace the first seam back yourself: click the smallest cell in the bottom row, then click your way up row by row. The machine can cut the rest.

body.en: The picture is 8 columns narrower, and neither letter is distorted at all: every seam slipped through unremarkable background. Squash the picture instead, and every letter gets squeezed thin.
This is called content-aware resizing (seam carving). When photo-editing software turns a landscape photo into a portrait one, this is how: a seam table, plus one trace back.
The edges you computed in Vision Complete became the robot’s terrain here. The two games share more than code underneath: they share ideas.

note.en: Seam carving: trace back from the smallest cell in the seam table’s bottom row, cut that seam out, and the picture is one column narrower.
